samples.text:
The diagram shows the stages of producing black tea. There is eight stages, from plucking the leaves to packing and exporting.

Firstly, the top two leaves and a bud are picked by hand. Then the leaves are spread on racks for 12–18 hours, this is called withering. After that the leaves are rolled for breaking the cell walls.

Next, the leaves are left for oxidation. In this stage, the colour of leaves change to copper-brown and it takes 1–3 hours. Then the leaves are dried with hot air at 120°C, and this stops the oxidation.

In the sixth stage, the leaves are sieved and sorted by the size. After that, professional tasters check the samples of tea to see if it is good. Finally, the tea is packed in sacks which have foil inside and it is exported.

Overall, black tea production has many stages and some of them take a lot of hours, for example withering. The process starts with picking leaves by hand and ends with export to other countries.
samples.why: Overview placed at the end and fairly general · all stages and figures covered accurately · repetitive linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, article and preposition errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the process of making black tea, from picking the leaves to packing the finished product.

Overall, there are eight stages in this linear process. The early stages mainly involve changing the physical state of the leaves, while the later ones focus on checking quality and preparing the tea for export. The process begins with hand-picking and ends with the tea being packed for export. Withering is the longest of the stages for which a time is given.

To begin with, the top two leaves and a bud are plucked by hand. They are then spread on racks to wither for 12 to 18 hours, after which they are rolled in order to break the cell walls. During the oxidation stage, the leaves turn a copper-brown colour over a period of one to three hours.

This process is stopped by drying the leaves with hot air at a temperature of 120°C. The dried leaves are then sieved and graded according to size, and samples are checked by professional tasters. Finally, the tea are packed in foil-lined sacks, ready to be exported.
samples.why: Clear overview grouping early and later stages · figures accurate and compared · logical progression with passive forms · some less common vocabulary (wither, graded) · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
The diagram charts the eight stages involved in the production of black tea, from harvesting the leaves to preparing them for export.

In broad terms, the first half of the process transforms the fresh leaves, whereas the second half is concerned with quality control and packaging. The process begins with leaves being picked by hand and ends with the finished tea being packed for shipment overseas. Withering, at 12–18 hours, is considerably lengthier than oxidation, which takes only one to three hours.

Production begins with plucking, a delicate task in which the top two leaves and a bud are picked by hand. These are then laid out on racks to wither before being rolled, a step which breaks down their cell walls. The rolled leaves are left to oxidise, gradually turning copper-brown, until this reaction is halted by a stream of hot air at 120°C.

Once dried, the leaves are sieved so that they can be sorted and graded by size. Samples are subsequently evaluated by professional tasters, and in the final stage the tea is packed into foil-lined sacks ready for export.
samples.why: Well-judged overview dividing the process and comparing stage durations · figures used selectively · cohesion managed fluently · precise vocabulary (halted, evaluated) · wide range of structures, error-free.
